diet: Mostly seagrass and algae as an adult
fact: It is named not for its shell but for the greenish colour of its body fat, a result of its plant diet.
range: Tropical and subtropical seas worldwide, including Guam's reefs
sourceNote: IUCN moved the global population from Endangered to Least Concern in October 2025; regional subpopulations differ.

diet: Mainly sponges, plus soft corals and other invertebrates
fact: It is one of very few animals that feed on sponges, many of which are toxic or packed with glassy spicules.
sourceNote: IUCN Red List (Critically Endangered).

diet: Zooplankton filtered from the water
fact: Mantas visit cleaning stations, where small wrasses pick parasites off them. Around Guam, researchers have also watched reef mantas feed on fish spawn.
range: Tropical and subtropical Indo-Pacific coasts and islands
sourceNote: Size is typical disc width (up to ~5 m). Guam spawn-feeding: University of Guam / Manta Trust research (J. Hartup).

diet: Small fishes, crustaceans and cephalopods
fact: It often patrols water so shallow that its black-tipped dorsal fin breaks the surface.
range: Shallow reefs of the tropical Indo-Pacific
sourceNote: IUCN 2020 global reassessment of reef sharks (Vulnerable).

diet: Fishes, octopuses and crustaceans, hunted at night in reef crevices
fact: Unlike many sharks, it can lie still on the bottom and pump water over its gills. It spends much of the day resting in caves or on sand.
sourceNote: IUCN 2020 (Vulnerable). Usually seen at 8–40 m.

diet: Mostly sponges, plus algae and small invertebrates
fact: It is the only living member of its family, the Zanclidae.
sourceNote: Often seen in pairs or small groups.

diet: Live coral and algae, bitten off with fused, beak-like teeth
fact: It is the largest of all parrotfishes. Overfishing has made it rare on Guam's reefs.
sourceNote: NOAA notes near-disappearance from Guam due to overexploitation.

diet: Molluscs, crustaceans, sea urchins and fishes
fact: It is one of the few predators of the coral-eating crown-of-thorns starfish.
range: Indo-Pacific coral reefs; now rarely seen around Guam
sourceNote: Can exceed 2 m. NOAA surveys found it uncommon to rare in the Marianas.

diet: Plankton, and algae as adults
fact: Like all surgeonfishes, it carries a scalpel-sharp spine on each side of the tail base.
sourceNote: Grows to about 31 cm.

diet: Zooplankton and algae
fact: Its colour varies with its host anemone: fish living in some carpet anemones are almost black.
range: Western and central Pacific, including the Marianas
sourceNote: Hosts include Heteractis crispa and Stichodactyla mertensii.

diet: Small fishes and crustaceans, herded with its fan-like fins
fact: Native to the Indo-Pacific, it has become a damaging invasive species in the western Atlantic and Caribbean.
sourceNote: Venomous dorsal spines.

diet: Sugars from symbiotic algae in its mantle, plus filtered plankton
fact: Its vivid mantle is a garden: algae living inside it photosynthesise and share their food with the clam.
sourceNote: IUCN 2024 (Least Concern). The larger T. gigas no longer occurs around Guam.

diet: Crabs, shrimps and small fishes
fact: Unusually for an octopus, it hunts in daylight, changing colour and skin texture in a fraction of a second.
sourceNote: Size is arm span; the mantle is about 16 cm.

diet: Zooplankton
fact: Schools hover above branching corals and dive into them for cover when threatened.
sourceNote: IUCN assessed 2021 (Least Concern).

diet: Parasites and mucus picked from other fishes
fact: It runs a cleaning station visited by fish far larger than itself, including mantas, which let it work around their mouths and gills.
sourceNote: Stations are often run by a pair or a small group.

diet: Fishes, squid and crustaceans
fact: It was the first shark known to perform a threat display: back hunched, pectoral fins lowered, swimming in exaggerated side-to-side arcs.
sourceNote: Threat display described in the scientific literature since the 1970s.

diet: Fishes
fact: By day it gathers in large, slowly circling schools; it hunts mostly at night.
sourceNote: Named for the dark chevron marks on its flanks.

diet: Fishes, crustaceans and cephalopods
fact: The largest of the trevallies, it often hunts along reef edges, sometimes in small groups.
sourceNote: Can reach about 1.7 m.

diet: Clams, snails and crustaceans dug from the sand and crushed with plate-like teeth
fact: It was long treated as part of the spotted eagle ray; genetic work separated the Indo-Pacific population as its own species.
sourceNote: Size is disc width. IUCN (Kyne et al.).

diet: Fishes and crustaceans, hunted mostly at night
fact: Its slow, rhythmic gaping is not a threat: the moray is pumping water over its gills.
sourceNote: One of the largest morays by weight.

diet: Plankton caught by thousands of tiny polyps
fact: Sea fans grow across the prevailing current so their polyps can filter as much water as possible.
sourceNote: A gorgonian (soft coral). Size is fan width.

diet: Zooplankton such as copepods and krill
fact: Among the most abundant vertebrates on Earth, many lanternfishes rise toward the surface each night to feed, part of the largest daily migration on the planet.
sourceNote: Identified to family; species need a specimen.

diet: Small crustaceans and other zooplankton
fact: Light organs along its belly match the faint glow from above and erase its silhouette, a trick called counter-illumination.
sourceNote: Deeper by day, shallower at night.

diet: Scavenges crustaceans and carrion
fact: It adjusts its buoyancy by moving fluid in and out of the gas-filled chambers of its shell.
sourceNote: Range spans the Philippines and Palau to Fiji and Australia; records close to the Marianas are scarce. Listed as threatened under the US ESA.

diet: Fishes, rays, squid and carrion
fact: Most sharks have five pairs of gill slits; this ancient lineage has six.
range: Tropical and temperate oceans worldwide; filmed near Guam in 2016
sourceNote: NOAA Okeanos Explorer sighting at Santa Rosa Reef, south of Guam (2016). Grows to about 5 m.

diet: Mainly deep-water squid
fact: Its clicks are among the loudest sounds made by any animal, and it uses them to find prey in total darkness.
range: All oceans; seen regularly around the Mariana Islands
sourceNote: Females about 11 m, males about 16 m. Dives beyond 1,000 m are routine.

diet: Small crustaceans and fishes caught on trailing stinging tentacles
fact: A siphonophore is not one animal but a colony of specialised clones: some swim, some feed, some reproduce. Some species exceed 40 m.
sourceNote: Identified to order; colonies are too fragile to collect for species ID.

diet: Plankton, including other comb jellies
fact: The shimmering rainbows on a comb jelly are not its own light: they come from light diffracting off rows of beating cilia.
sourceNote: Many comb jellies also bioluminesce, but their rainbow shimmer is diffraction, not light they make.

diet: Marine snow, gathered on two long filaments
fact: Despite its name, it is a gentle drifter that feeds on marine snow, the debris sinking from above.
range: Tropical and temperate oceans, in low-oxygen water
sourceNote: Diet: Hoving & Robison (2012).

diet: Fishes and crustaceans lured close by its glowing esca
fact: The glowing lure on its head is lit by bioluminescent bacteria living inside it.
sourceNote: Size is for females; males are far smaller.

diet: Fishes, crustaceans and squid
fact: Relative to its body it has some of the largest teeth of any fish, and sockets beside its brain let it close its mouth over the longest fangs.
sourceNote: Recorded deeper than 4,000 m.

diet: Small crustaceans, scooped up in an enormous, loosely hinged mouth
fact: Its whip-like tail ends in a small light organ that glows pink to red.
sourceNote: Also called the pelican eel.

diet: Copepods and small fishes
fact: It shines a red light most deep-sea animals cannot see, and uses a chlorophyll-based pigment from its food to see that red light itself.
sourceNote: Douglas et al., Nature (1998).

diet: Small crustaceans and other drifting animals
fact: When attacked it sets off a spinning ring of blue light, a 'burglar alarm' that may draw a bigger predator to its attacker.
sourceNote: Display described by NOAA Ocean Exploration (E. Widder).

diet: Fishes and other squid
fact: The first photographs of a live giant squid in its habitat were taken in 2004 near Japan's Ogasawara Islands, at about 900 m.
sourceNote: Kubodera & Mori (2005). Size includes the long feeding tentacles.

diet: Food made by bacteria living in its gills
fact: Bacteria living in its gills turn chemicals from the vent fluid, such as sulfide, into food for the mussel.
range: Western Pacific and Indian Ocean vents, including NW Eifuku on the Mariana arc
sourceNote: B. brevior (described with NW Eifuku material) is now a synonym (Zootaxa 2022).

diet: Mostly bacteria growing on and around the vents
fact: Its genus name means 'dancing shrimp', after the restless way they move around the vents.
sourceNote: Described by Martin & Hessler (1990) from the Alice Springs vent field.

diet: Scavenger and predator of other vent animals
fact: It appears to live only on the Mariana Trough vents, where it forages among the snail beds around vent openings.
sourceNote: Hessler & Martin (1989); review in Zoosystema (2018).

diet: Food made by bacteria living in its gill
fact: The most abundant animal at many Mariana Trough vents, it carries bristly hairs on its shell.
range: Endemic to the Mariana Trough vents
sourceNote: IUCN 2019 (Vulnerable, D2), citing deep-sea mining risk.

diet: Crustaceans and worms, swallowed whole
fact: One was filmed at 6,957 m in the Java Trench, the deepest octopus ever recorded.
sourceNote: Jamieson & Vecchione, Marine Biology (2020).

diet: Small crustaceans drifting past in the current
fact: It stands on three hugely lengthened fin rays, sometimes over a metre tall, facing into the current to intercept prey.
range: Atlantic, Indian and western central Pacific oceans
sourceNote: Depth range per FishBase.

diet: Organic matter in the surface sediment
fact: Its 'legs' are enlarged tube feet, moved by pumping water in and out of them.
range: Deep seafloor in all major oceans
sourceNote: May be a complex of several species (Museums Victoria).

diet: Bacteria and particles filtered from the water
fact: Its skeleton is made of silica, glass, and it anchors itself in soft mud with a tuft of long glassy fibres.
sourceNote: A hexactinellid (glass) sponge.

diet: Organic particles and small animals
fact: Brittle stars move by rowing with their flexible arms rather than walking on tube feet like sea stars.
range: All oceans, from shallows to trenches
sourceNote: Identified to class. Size is arm span.

diet: Scavenged carrion and small animals
fact: It is the only grenadier known from the hadal zone, recorded down to about 7,000 m in the Mariana Trench.
sourceNote: FishBase gives a maximum length of 63 cm; usual depth 3,400–5,800 m.

diet: Mostly amphipods and other small crustaceans
fact: Described in 2017 from fish caught between 6,898 and 7,966 m, it was then the deepest-caught fish with confirmed depth.
sourceNote: Gerringer et al., Zootaxa (2017); filmed at 8,178 m.

diet: Carrion and sunken plant debris
fact: Its gut enzymes can turn wood and other plant debris into sugar, even at the pressure of the Challenger Deep.
range: Western Pacific trenches, including the Challenger Deep
sourceNote: Kobayashi et al., PLoS ONE (2012). Large for an amphipod ('gigas').

diet: Particles trapped from the surrounding water and sediment
fact: Each is a single giant cell. In the Mariana Trench they have been seen as deep as 10,641 m.
sourceNote: Sirena Deep observations (2011), confirmed by A. Gooday.

diet: Organic matter in the sediment
fact: Sea cucumbers are echinoderms, relatives of sea stars and urchins, that slowly hoover food from the seafloor sediment.
sourceNote: A Paelopatides sp. was collected at 6,633 m in the neighbouring Yap Trench.
